Honestly, watch out for the meeting transcripts where someone's been having full conversations with ChatGPT instead of their actual colleagues.

This matters to digital workplace pros because the hardware infrastructure powering workplace AI tools, collaboration platforms, and automation is about to get competitive in ways that could drive down costs and improve performance across the board. Honestly, it's refreshing to see someone challenge Nvidia's comfortable dominance, though I'll believe AMD has truly moved beyond "second fiddle" status when enterprises actually start standardizing on their chips at scale.

ai-at-work.title: AMD’s Helios strategy turns the GPU battle into a systems contest

ai-at-work.dwp_take: AMD is shifting from selling individual GPUs to selling complete, validated rack-scale systems that work out of the box for massive AI workloads. This matters because it signals that enterprise buyers are done tinkering with components and want integrated solutions they can deploy fast, which changes how digital workplace infrastructure gets procured and managed. After three decades watching IT shops cobble together Frankenstein systems, I'm genuinely relieved someone finally figured out that enterprises want to buy confidence, not puzzles.

The real news here is that we're hitting the point where "good enough AI" costs so little that not using it is starting to look wasteful, which means your boss will definitely want to talk about this at the next meeting.

After three decades in this space, I'll say it: when enterprise AI gets cheaper without losing capability, people actually start building things instead of just talking about it in meetings.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Tech leaders are saying three types of workers will thrive when AI agents run more of the day-to-day business operations. tools-tech.title: I tested a $14 emergency radio with solar and hand-crank power - it's in my survival kit now

tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone reviewed a cheap emergency radio that actually does its job when normal power fails, combining solar charging, hand-crank backup, and weather alerts in one device. Digital workplace folks should care because this is a real-world reminder that our always-on infrastructure is fragile and contingency planning beats wishful thinking when disaster hits. Here's the thing though: we spend fortunes on redundant cloud systems and backup generators for the office, but most of us couldn't operate for an hour if the internet actually went down.

digital-culture.title: AI may finally make ‘women’s work’ valuable. But will women benefit?
digital-culture.excerpt: For years, economists have predicted that artificial intelligence would hollow out the labor market. Machines would write the code, analyze the contracts, draft the emails, and automate the work that
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is reporting that AI might finally elevate traditionally undervalued "women's work" like caregiving and mentoring because machines can't replicate those human skills, though the piece questions whether women will actually benefit economically from this shift. This matters to digital workplace pros because it forces us to reckon with whether our tech implementations are genuinely creating more equitable work or just reshuffling who does what for similar pay. The irony is delicious: we spent decades automating "women's work" away, and now that it's scarce, suddenly it's valuable, which tells you everything about how the market values labor rather than the actual work itself.

digital-culture.title: Here’s how Meta decides who to lay off—and it claims to not use AI
digital-culture.excerpt: Twenty-six employees at Meta who were recently laid off made a bold claim in a lawsuit last week: They alleged the company had used AI to select people for layoffs, disproportionately impacting people
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta claims it doesn't use AI to pick who gets laid off, but 26 employees are suing anyway, alleging the company's selection process disproportionately hit people on leave and those with disabilities. This matters because every company with workforce management tools needs to understand that "we didn't use AI for this" isn't a defense if your algorithm-adjacent processes produce discriminatory outcomes. Funny how the company that built its empire on algorithmic decision-making suddenly wants us to believe their layoff decisions were totally human-driven intuition.

digital-culture.title: Forget layoffs: This quiet workplace tactic is shucking headcounts without anyone noticing
digital-culture.excerpt: Employees across the workforce often collectively hold their breath in dread whenever another big company announces layoffs attributed to the work automating capabilities of artificial intelligence (A
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are quietly cutting headcount by simply not replacing people who leave, rather than announcing formal layoffs. This matters because it creates the same job insecurity and burnout as explicit layoffs, except HR gets to pretend everything's fine while remaining staff absorb the work. It's the corporate equivalent of slowly turning down the thermostat and hoping nobody notices they're freezing.

digital-culture.title: This is the impact that AI will have on entry-level work and development
digital-culture.excerpt: As AI continues to automate routine tasks, some progressive organizations are shifting early-career roles to handle complex work that requires judgment. As a result, junior employees need to navigate
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company reports that AI is pushing entry-level work toward complex problem-solving instead of routine tasks, but most companies haven't updated their training programs to match this shift. This matters because digital workplace leaders now need to completely rethink onboarding, mentorship, and skill development for junior staff who are expected to handle sophisticated work without the traditional learning runway. The irony is we're all scrambling to train people for jobs that look nothing like the jobs we trained people for five years ago, and nobody's really figured out how to do that well yet.
